15060: A spyglass is a small, handheld tube-shaped instrument that makes faraway objects appear much closer and larger when you look through it. Think of it as a compact, one-handed telescope — the kind you've probably seen a pirate or a ship's captain hold up to one eye in movies or books.

A spyglass is a slim, cylindrical (tube-shaped) device, usually made of metal or leather-covered metal. It is designed to be held comfortably in one hand.

One of its most recognizable features is that it collapses and extends. The tube is made of two or more sections that slide into each other. When you're not using it, you push the sections together so it becomes short and compact — easy to tuck into a pocket or a belt. When you want to use it, you pull the sections out so the tube becomes longer. This sliding, extending design is called a telescoping design (which is actually where the word "telescope" gets its meaning too — something that slides together like a collapsing tube).

It has a small lens at one end (the end you point at what you want to see) and a viewing hole at the other end (the end you hold up to your eye).

The lenses inside a spyglass bend light in a clever way. When light from a distant object enters the far end of the spyglass, the lenses capture that light and rearrange it so that, by the time it reaches your eye, the object looks much larger and nearer than it actually is.

For example, if you're standing on a cliff and a ship is 2 kilometres away, with your naked eye it might look like a tiny speck. But through a spyglass, it might look as though it's only 100 metres away — close enough to see the people on deck, the colour of the sails, or whether the ship is friend or foe.

You hold a spyglass up to one eye (not both eyes — that's important). You close or ignore the other eye, look through the viewing hole, and point the instrument toward whatever you want to observe. You may need to adjust (pull out or push in the tube slightly) to bring the image into sharp focus, because the right length varies depending on how far away the object is.

The act of pointing a spyglass at something is often described as "training" it on something. For example: "He trained his spyglass on the approaching ship." You can also "raise," "lift," or "put a spyglass to your eye."

The spyglass was an essential tool for centuries, particularly from the 1600s through the 1800s. The people who used it most commonly were:

  • Sailors and naval officers — to spot land, rocks, enemy ships, or approaching storms from the deck of a ship, long before those things came dangerously close.
  • Ship captains and pirates — to identify other vessels at sea. This is why the spyglass is so heavily associated with pirate imagery in popular culture.
  • Military commanders and scouts — to observe enemy troop movements, fortifications, or terrain from a safe distance without being seen themselves.
  • Explorers — to survey unfamiliar land or coastlines from a distance.
  • Lookouts — sailors posted high up on a ship's mast ("in the crow's nest") would use a spyglass to scan the horizon for anything significant.

The core idea behind all these uses is the same: seeing something from far away without having to go near it — whether for safety, strategy, or surprise.
How It Differs From Similar Objects

Understanding what a spyglass is not helps sharpen what it is:

Spyglass vs. Telescope:
A telescope is a much larger, far more powerful optical instrument — usually too big to hold by hand, often mounted on a stand or a tripod. Telescopes are designed primarily for looking at celestial objects (stars, planets, the moon) and can magnify objects thousands of times. A spyglass, by contrast, is small, portable, and designed for looking at things on Earth or at sea — not the night sky. Its magnification is modest compared to a telescope.

Spyglass vs. Binoculars:
Binoculars are the instrument you're probably more familiar with today — the double-tubed device you hold up to both eyes at the same time. Binoculars give you a wider, more comfortable, three-dimensional view because both your eyes work together. A spyglass, on the other hand, uses only one eye. For this reason, a spyglass is called monocular (mono = one), while binoculars are binocular (bi = two). A spyglass is also generally more compact and simpler than binoculars.

Here are a few examples that show how the word is naturally used:

  • The captain lifted his spyglass to his eye and watched the distant coast slowly come into focus.
  • From the crow's nest, the lookout peered through his spyglass and shouted, "Ship ahoy!"
  • The old pirate kept his battered spyglass tucked inside his coat at all times.
  • She extended the spyglass and trained it on the ridge, trying to spot the scouts.
  • Through the spyglass, what had appeared to be a cluster of rocks turned out to be a small fishing village.

The word "spyglass" is considered somewhat old-fashioned today. In everyday modern language, the same kind of device is more often called a monocular or a spotting scope. These modern versions are used by birdwatchers, hikers, hunters, sailors, and military personnel.

However, the word "spyglass" is far from dead. You'll encounter it regularly in:

  • Historical novels and literature set in past centuries
  • Pirate-themed stories, movies, and games
  • Nautical and maritime writing
  • Fantasy and adventure fiction
  • Casual, poetic, or nostalgic contexts where someone wants to evoke a sense of old-world adventure

The word carries a strong flavour of adventure, the sea, and a bygone era — which is part of why writers and storytellers still love using it.

A spyglass is a small, collapsible, handheld instrument with lenses inside a tube that you hold up to one eye to see distant objects as though they are much closer — historically used by sailors, pirates, scouts, and explorers.
15061: The word "squab" (noun) has a few separate meanings, but one is by far the most important and most commonly encountered.

A squab is a baby pigeon — specifically one that is still in the nest and has not yet flown or learned to fly on its own. This typically means a pigeon chick that is roughly 25 to 30 days old.

Here's what makes a squab special and distinct from an ordinary pigeon:

  • At this stage, the bird has grown to nearly full size, but its flight muscles are still undeveloped because it hasn't used them yet.
  • Its meat is therefore extremely tender and soft, unlike the tougher, chewier meat of an adult pigeon.
  • The meat is dark, rich, and full of flavour — far more so than common poultry like chicken.

Because of these qualities, squab has been prized as a delicacy (a rare, special, high-quality food) for centuries across many cultures — French cuisine, Chinese cuisine, Middle Eastern cuisine, and others all have traditional squab dishes.

In a practical, everyday context: If you ever see "squab" on the menu of a fine-dining or upscale restaurant, it simply means a young pigeon prepared as a dish. It is not uncommon — it appears regularly in gourmet cooking.

One important nuance: in culinary use, squabs are almost always from domesticated pigeons raised specifically for food (not wild pigeons from the street). These birds are kept in controlled environments and harvested young, before they ever fly, which is what guarantees their tenderness.
Secondary Meaning: A Thick Cushion or Padded Seat

The word "squab" can also refer to a thick, heavily stuffed cushion — the kind used to pad the seat or back of a sofa, chair, or old-fashioned vehicle like a carriage or early automobile. Think of the plush, puffy removable seat pad on a bench or the cushioned interior of a horse-drawn coach.

This meaning is fairly uncommon in modern everyday speech, but you may encounter it in older literature, interior design writing, or when describing antique furniture and vehicles. If someone says a chair has a "squab cushion," they mean it has a thick, padded cushion attached to the seat or backrest.
Tertiary Meaning: A Short, Fat Person

Informally and somewhat dated (meaning it was more common in older times), "squab" could be used to describe a person who is short and plump or fat. The connection is visual: a baby pigeon is round, chubby, and compact — so the word was extended to describe people with a similar shape.

This usage is rarely heard in modern English and would mostly appear in older texts or literature. You are very unlikely to need to use it yourself, but it's worth knowing so you aren't puzzled if you come across it.

If you're wondering why one word carries such different meanings, notice the common thread: all three senses of "squab" involve something soft, round, and compact — a plump baby bird, a fat cushion, a stout person. The word has this sense of soft fullness running through it.

When you encounter "squab"...It almost certainly means...
On a restaurant menu or in a recipeA young, tender pigeon raised for eating
In a description of furniture or old vehiclesA thick, stuffed cushion
In old literature or writingPossibly a short, fat person

The first meaning — the young pigeon — is the one you need to know most. The other two are supplementary knowledge.
15062:
A squabble is a small, noisy argument about something that is not very important. Think of it as a minor quarrel — it is real and heated in the moment, but it is too petty and trivial to be called a serious fight or conflict.

The key idea is smallness. The disagreement is real, the people involved are genuinely annoyed at each other, but the thing they are fighting about is usually not worth getting that worked up over.
The Essential Qualities of a Squabble

A squabble always has these features:

  1. Trivial cause. The thing being argued about is minor — who ate the last biscuit, whose turn it is to do the dishes, who gets to hold the TV remote. The subject is small. This is the most important quality of a squabble.
  2. Noisy and heated. Despite being about something minor, the people involved raise their voices, interrupt each other, or bicker loudly. It is not a calm, quiet disagreement.
  3. Short-lived. Squabbles tend to flare up and die down quickly. They do not go on for days or weeks like a deep grudge or a serious dispute.
  4. Petty. The word "petty" means unnecessarily concerned about small, unimportant things. A squabble is petty by nature — both in cause and in the behaviour of the people involved.

• "The two brothers had a squabble over who got the window seat in the car."
  • "Their squabble about the grocery bill lasted only a few minutes before they both laughed it off."
  • "Every Sunday, there was the usual squabble among the cousins over which game to play."
  • "The meeting was delayed because of a squabble between two committee members over a minor procedural point."

Notice that in every example, the argument is real but the subject is small or petty. No one is in serious danger, no great harm is being done, and the disagreement is not life-altering.
How Serious Is a Squabble? (The Scale)

It helps to understand where a squabble sits on the scale of conflict:

Minor end → Serious end:

Disagreement → Squabble / Spat / Tiff → Argument → Quarrel → Fight → Feud → War

A squabble sits near the mild end. It is more intense than a simple "disagreement" (which can be calm and silent), but far less serious than a "quarrel," a "feud," or a "conflict." A squabble is never violent, never deeply bitter, and never long-lasting.
How Is It Different from Similar Words?

There are words that come very close to "squabble," but each has a slightly different flavour:

  • Argument — Broader and more neutral. An argument can be minor or very serious. A squabble is always minor.
  • Quarrel — More serious and more bitter than a squabble. A quarrel can damage a relationship and linger for a long time.
  • Spat — Very similar to a squabble. A spat is a brief, minor disagreement, often between people who are close (like friends or partners). The key difference is that a spat emphasises briefness, while a squabble emphasises pettiness and noise.
  • Tiff — Also very similar. A tiff usually implies a slight emotional hurt between people who care about each other. It is softer and more personal than a squabble.
  • Bickering — This is ongoing, repeated petty arguing. Where a squabble is a single event ("they had a squabble"), bickering is a continuous back-and-forth ("they kept bickering all afternoon"). Bickering is the process; a squabble is a distinct incident.
  • Dispute — More formal and often official. Disputes happen between companies, governments, or parties in legal matters. You would not call a legal case a "squabble" unless you were being dismissive.

This is important: the word "squabble" itself is slightly dismissive and even mildly humorous.

When someone calls an argument a "squabble," they are quietly signalling that the whole thing is not worth taking seriously. It subtly mocks the people involved for getting worked up over something small. If you say, "They had a terrible conflict," you sound grave and serious. But if you say, "They had a squabble," you are almost rolling your eyes at the pettiness of it.

This means squabble is often used by an observer — someone watching from the outside, who can see that the argument is overblown. The people actually in the squabble may not think of it that way themselves.

The word is informal in register. You would use it in everyday speech and in casual writing, but you would not use it in formal writing (such as academic papers, legal documents, or official reports).
Common Collocations (How the Word Is Typically Used)

A "collocation" is a natural pairing — words that go together naturally in English.

  • "a petty squabble" (very common — reinforces the trivial nature)
  • "a minor squabble"
  • "a brief squabble"
  • "a squabble over something" (e.g., "a squabble over money," "a squabble over credit")
  • "a squabble between people" (e.g., "a squabble between siblings")
  • "break out into a squabble" (the squabble begins)
  • "settle a squabble" (end or resolve it)
When You Should — and Should Not — Use This Word

Use "squabble" when:

  • The argument is about something trivial or petty.
  • You want to suggest the disagreement is not very important.
  • The tone is informal or conversational.
  • You are describing a brief, noisy dispute that dies down quickly.

Do not use "squabble" when:

  • The conflict is serious, deep, or long-lasting.
  • Real harm is involved — emotional, physical, or legal.
  • You want to treat the dispute with gravity and respect.
  • You are writing formally.

For example, you would never call a war, a court case, or a bitter family breakdown a "squabble" — unless you are deliberately trivialising it for effect or irony.
The Complete Picture in One Sentence
A squabble is a noisy, petty, short-lived argument between two or more people about something trivial — real enough that voices are raised, but too minor and silly to be taken seriously.
15063: A squad is a small, organized group of people who share a common purpose, task, or identity. That single idea stretches across many different contexts — military, police, sports, and everyday life — but the core always stays the same: a small, tight group with something in common.
1. The Military Meaning (the original, formal use)

In the military, a squad is the smallest fighting unit in an army — typically around 8 to 13 soldiers who operate together under one leader (usually a corporal or sergeant). Think of it like this: an army is massive, but it is broken down into smaller and smaller groups. A squad is the smallest of those groups — the basic building block of military organization.

The squad was ordered to advance toward the hilltop.

Because it is so small, every soldier in a squad knows every other soldier personally. They train together, fight together, and depend on each other directly. This closeness is very much part of the word's feeling.
2. The Police and Emergency Services Meaning

In policing and emergency services, a squad refers to a specialized team formed for a specific job or mission.

The bomb squad was called to the scene.
The SWAT squad surrounded the building.
Detectives from the homicide squad investigated the case.

Here, the word highlights that these are not just any officers — they are a dedicated group with a specific expertise or duty. Common examples:

  • Bomb squad — experts who handle explosive devices
  • Narcotics squad — officers who deal with drug-related crimes
  • Flying squad — a fast-response police unit that can be deployed quickly anywhere
  • Death squad — an armed group (often illegal or state-sponsored) that carries out targeted killings; this phrase carries a very dark, serious tone

In sports, squad refers to the full pool of players available to a team — not just the ones playing in a match on a given day, but everyone selected for the team overall.

This is especially common in British English and in sports like football (soccer), cricket, and rugby.

The manager named his 23-man squad for the World Cup.
She was dropped from the national squad due to injury.

The key distinction here: a squad is bigger than the starting lineup or playing XI. If a football team has 23 players selected for a tournament, all 23 are the squad. Only 11 start the match — but all 23 are part of the squad.

So "making the squad" means you've been chosen as part of the group, but you might still be a substitute or not even play. It's an important step, but not the final one.

Outside of military, police, and sports, squad is used more loosely to mean any small group organized around a shared task or identity.

A cleaning squad moved through the stadium after the event.
A squad of journalists gathered outside the courthouse.

In this sense, it's just a convenient, slightly energetic word for "a small team of people doing something together."
5. The Modern Slang Meaning (very common today)

This is the meaning most young people use today. In casual, everyday language — especially in social media, pop culture, and conversation — your squad is your close circle of friends.

I'm going out with my squad tonight.
My squad always has my back.
We're a tight squad — we've known each other for years.

This use exploded in popular culture, particularly in the 2010s. The idea is that your squad isn't just any group of friends — it's your inner circle, the people you trust, hang out with regularly, and feel a strong bond with. It carries a sense of loyalty, closeness, and shared identity.

"Squad goals" is a phrase that grew out of this slang use. When you see a group of friends who look fun, stylish, supportive, or admirable, you might say "squad goals" — meaning "I want my own friend group to be like that."

Look at how close they all are. Squad goals.

Even though "squad" is used in very different settings, notice that the same core feelings run through all of them:

  • Small — a squad is never a massive crowd. It's intimate.
  • Organized or tight-knit — there's a sense of cohesion, shared purpose, or belonging.
  • Purposeful — squads don't just happen randomly; they form around something: a mission, a sport, a friendship.

This is why the word feels energetic and cool even in casual use. It carries a subtle sense of we are a unit, we belong together, we operate as one.
A Quick Summary of All the Uses

• Military: a small unit of soldiers (~8–13) — the smallest fighting group
  • Police/emergency: a specialized team for a specific task (bomb squad, SWAT squad, etc.)
  • Sports: the full roster of selected players for a team, larger than just the starting lineup
  • General informal: any small group doing something together
  • Modern slang: your close circle of friends; your inner group

If you ever hear or read "squad" and aren't sure which meaning is intended, ask yourself: What is the context — military, sports, police, or social life? The context will almost always make the meaning obvious. And whichever context it is, the word is pointing to the same thing: a small, bonded group with something in common.
15064:
A squadron is an organized, structured group of military people and their vehicles — usually aircraft, ships, or cavalry horses — that operate together as a single unit under one commander.

Think of it this way: just as a school has individual students grouped into classes, and classes grouped into grades, a military force groups its people and machines into units. A squadron is one such unit — not the smallest, not the largest, but a recognizable, mid-sized building block of a military organization.

The word almost always appears in military or formal contexts. It describes a unit, not just a crowd. The key idea is that these people and machines are organized, coordinated, and work together with a shared purpose under clear leadership.

1. In Air Forces (the most common modern use)

This is where you'll encounter the word most often today. In an air force, a squadron is a unit made up of a number of aircraft — typically somewhere between 12 and 24 aircraft, depending on the country and the mission — along with all the pilots, crew, and ground support staff who keep those aircraft flying.

A squadron in this context is a living, working team. It has its own identity, its own name or number (like "No. 1 Squadron" or "101st Fighter Squadron"), and its own commander. The people in it train together, deploy together, and carry out missions together.

For example, if a country needs to send jet fighters to protect its airspace, it doesn't send individual pilots flying independently — it sends a squadron: a coordinated unit with a chain of command, shared tactics, and a clear structure.

The commander of an air force squadron is often called a Squadron Leader (in some countries, like the UK and India, this is an actual official rank).

2. In Navies (historical and still used today)

In a navy, a squadron is a group of warships that sail and fight together under a single commander. It is smaller than a full fleet (which is the largest naval grouping) but larger than an individual ship.

Historically, navies divided their fleets into squadrons — for example, a fleet might have a "van squadron" (at the front), a "centre squadron" (in the middle), and a "rear squadron" (at the back) during a naval battle. Each squadron had its own admiral in command.

Today, navies still use the term. A squadron might be a group of destroyers, submarines, or patrol vessels assigned to operate together in a particular region or for a particular mission.

3. In Armies — Cavalry and Armored Units

In land armies, particularly in cavalry (soldiers who historically fought on horseback) and modern armored units (soldiers who operate tanks and armored vehicles), a squadron is equivalent to what infantry forces call a company.

An armored or cavalry squadron typically has around 100 to 200 soldiers and their vehicles. It is made up of several smaller units called troops (the cavalry equivalent of a platoon in infantry), and multiple squadrons together form a regiment.

So in this context:

  • A troop is the smallest unit.
  • Several troops form a squadron.
  • Several squadrons form a regiment.
How a Squadron Fits in the Bigger Picture

One of the most important things to understand about the word "squadron" is that it describes a level in a hierarchy. It is never the top level (a whole air force or fleet), and it is never the bottom level (a single aircraft or soldier). It sits in the middle — a manageable, cohesive unit that is large enough to carry out meaningful independent missions but small enough to be commanded closely and effectively.

Here's a rough sense of the hierarchy in an air force, from smallest to largest:

  • Section / Element — just a few aircraft or people
  • Flight — a small group of aircraft, a subdivision of a squadron
  • Squadron — the main operational unit (the focus of this word)
  • Group / Wing — made up of several squadrons
  • Command / Air Force — the entire organization

Every squadron has a commanding officer — a senior military officer who is responsible for the unit's training, discipline, readiness, and performance in the field. In many air forces, this person holds the rank of Squadron Leader (equivalent to a Major in army terms). In navies, a squadron is typically commanded by a commodore or a senior captain.

This commander is accountable for every person and every vehicle in the squadron.

Outside of strict military contexts, people sometimes use "squadron" to colorfully describe any group of things that move together in a coordinated or impressive way. For example:

  • "A squadron of motorcycles roared past."
  • "A squadron of journalists followed the politician everywhere."

In these cases, the speaker is borrowing the word's sense of organized, collective movement to make their description feel more vivid or dramatic. This is an informal use, and in formal or technical writing, "squadron" is kept for its military meaning.

• The air force dispatched a squadron of fighter jets to patrol the border.
  • The squadron's commanding officer briefed his pilots before the mission.
  • After the naval exercise, the squadron returned to its home port.
  • The cavalry squadron charged across the field in tight formation.
  • Three squadrons were combined to form a single wing for the operation.

A squadron is a formally organized military unit of aircraft, ships, or cavalry/armored soldiers that operates together under a single commander. It is a mid-level unit — larger than a flight or a troop, but smaller than a wing or a regiment. In everyday modern life, you will most often encounter the word in the context of air forces, where it refers to a group of military aircraft and their crew. The word carries a strong sense of structure, coordination, and collective identity: a squadron is not a random gathering — it is a team, trained and organized to act as one.
15065:
Squalid describes something that is extremely dirty, neglected, and miserable — especially in a way that feels degrading or shameful. It is almost always used to describe conditions that are not just unclean, but deeply depressing and unfit for a decent human life.

Think of it this way: if a room is "dirty," someone forgot to clean it. If a room is "squalid," it looks like no one has cared about it for a very long time — it is falling apart, stained, overcrowded, and suffocating. There is a sense of hopelessness to it.

1. Physical Squalor — Describing Places and Living Conditions

This is the most common use. When you call a place squalid, you are saying it is:

  • Extremely dirty and filthy
  • Poorly maintained and neglected
  • Associated with poverty, overcrowding, and misery
  • Unfit for any decent standard of living

The word carries far more weight than simply "dirty" or "messy." It suggests that the condition has gone on for a long time, that nobody has taken care of it, and that living there would be deeply unpleasant and humiliating.

Examples:

  • "The workers were packed into a squalid room with no windows, a broken toilet, and rats running across the floor."
  • "The refugees were forced to live in squalid camps — muddy, overcrowded, and without clean water."
  • "He grew up in a squalid apartment where the walls were black with mold and the heating never worked."

Notice that in each case, the word does more than describe dirt. It paints a picture of suffering, neglect, and indignity.

2. Moral Squalor — Describing Behavior, Situations, or Actions

Squalid can also describe human behavior, situations, or events that are morally corrupt, shameful, or disgracefully low. Here, there is no physical dirt involved — the "filth" is metaphorical. You are saying that something is ethically rotten or socially degrading.

Examples:

  • "The investigation revealed a squalid story of bribes, lies, and betrayal."
  • "The whole affair was squalid — a powerful man abusing his position to exploit vulnerable people."
  • "The negotiation collapsed in a squalid argument over money."

In this sense, squalid implies that something decent and noble has been dragged down into something base and disgraceful. It is not merely "bad" — it is contemptibly, shamefully bad.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

This is important: squalid is not a neutral word. When you use it, you are not just describing a fact — you are also expressing a strong feeling of disgust, pity, or moral disapproval. It is a word that carries judgment.

Compare:

  • "The house was untidy." — Neutral, mild.
  • "The house was dirty." — Factual, slightly negative.
  • "The house was squalid." — Strong, loaded with disgust and a sense that something has gone very wrong.

Because of this emotional weight, squalid is a word that writers use deliberately when they want the reader to feel repelled or disturbed.
How It Differs from Similar Words

WordWhat it adds
  • Dirty simply means not clean. It has no strong emotional charge and no connection to poverty or neglect. Your hands can be dirty after gardening.
  • Filthy is a stronger form of dirty — very unclean. But it still describes just physical dirtiness without the deeper implications of degradation.
  • Grimy suggests a surface layer of grime, grease, or smudges — often from work or pollution. It is descriptive, not deeply judgmental.
  • Squalid goes furthest. It combines physical filth with neglect, poverty, human misery, and a sense of moral degradation. You would never call dirty hands "squalid." You would use squalid to describe a slum, a prison cell, or a scandal.

In real writing and speech, you will most often see squalid used with words like:

  • Squalid conditions — the most common pairing; used to describe housing, camps, prisons, or any environment people are forced to live in
  • Squalid flat / room / apartment — a physical living space that is dirty and neglected
  • Squalid affair / scandal — a shameful and morally corrupt event
  • Squalid little deal / arrangement — something dishonest or underhanded done for petty gain
  • Squalid existence — a life of poverty, degradation, and misery
Register — When and Where Is It Used?

Squalid is a moderately formal word. You will encounter it often in:

  • Journalism (especially reporting on poverty, housing, or political scandals)
  • Literary fiction (to describe grim living conditions)
  • Social commentary and essays

In everyday casual speech, people might simply say "disgusting," "filthy," or "shameful" instead. But when someone does use squalid in conversation, they are being deliberately emphatic — they want to communicate not just a fact, but a strong sense of moral or physical revulsion.
Squalid = so dirty, neglected, or morally corrupt that it is not just unpleasant — it is degrading and shameful.
15066: To squall means to cry or scream very loudly, harshly, and without control. It describes a raw, sharp, piercing kind of wailing — the kind that cuts through the air and can't easily be ignored.

"Squall" is not just any cry. It carries a specific character:

  • Loud — not a soft weep or a quiet sob, but a full-throated, noisy outburst
  • Harsh and unmusical — the sound is grating or sharp, not smooth or soft
  • Uncontrolled — the person (or creature) squalling is not holding anything back; the sound pours out raw and unrestrained
  • Prolonged or repeated — it often suggests not just a single yelp but a sustained or repeated bout of screaming or wailing

Think of it as the sonic equivalent of a storm — sudden, intense, and hard to miss.

Babies and young children are the most classic subjects of this verb. When a newborn is hungry, cold, in pain, or simply wants attention, it will squall — screaming with its whole body in that raw, unfiltered way only infants can.

But the word isn't limited to babies. It can apply to:

  • Older children throwing a tantrum
  • Adults in extreme emotional distress, fear, or anger (though this use is less common and often slightly ironic or literary)
  • Animals — especially cats, birds, or other creatures making harsh, loud cries

Squalling is usually driven by:

  • Pain — a child who falls and hurts itself may squall
  • Hunger or discomfort — the classic baby scenario
  • Fear or distress — overwhelming emotion that breaks through any composure
  • Anger — especially in children who haven't yet learned to manage frustration

1. The baby squalled all night, keeping the entire household awake.
    → The baby cried loudly and without stopping through the night.
  2. He squalled in pain when the doctor cleaned the wound.
    → He let out a sharp, uncontrolled cry of pain.
  3. The toddler squalled and kicked when her mother tried to take the toy away.
    → She screamed loudly and fiercely, without any restraint.
  4. Cats squalled on the rooftop, their sounds echoing down the street.
    → The cats made loud, harsh, piercing cries.
  5. She squalled at the top of her lungs when she saw the spider.
    → She screamed loudly and sharply out of fear.
How is it different from similar words?

This is where the word really becomes clear — by seeing what it is not:

  • Cry — the broadest and gentlest word. You can cry silently, softly, or in a dignified way. Squalling is always loud and raw.
  • Wail — loud and mournful, like grief or despair. A wail is more sustained and has a musical, almost lamenting quality. Squalling is harsher and less musical — more of a protest or pain response than a lament.
  • Shriek — typically a single, sudden burst of very high-pitched sound, usually from shock or sudden fear. A shriek is sharp and brief. Squalling tends to go on and on.
  • Howl — powerful and long, like a wolf or someone in deep anguish. Howling has a certain wild, sustained quality; squalling is more chaotic and uncontrolled.
  • Whimper — the opposite end of the scale: soft, weak, subdued. Squalling is nothing like whimpering.

If you had to place squalling on a scale, it sits at the loud, harsh, uncontrolled, raw end — especially associated with the helpless urgency of infants or the unfiltered emotion of someone overwhelmed.
A note on the noun form

Since the verb and noun are closely related and you'll encounter them together: when "squall" is used as a noun in reference to sound, it means a loud, harsh cry or screaming outburst (e.g., "a squall of protest from the crowd"). You may also know "squall" as a noun meaning a sudden violent windstorm — that's a completely separate meaning, unrelated to the verb sense you've just learned.
To squall = to cry or scream in a loud, raw, harsh, uncontrolled way — the kind of sound a hungry newborn makes at 3 a.m., or what escapes a person when pain or fear overwhelms them completely.
15067:
Squalor means a state of extreme, filthy, and degrading dirtiness — especially one that has built up over a long time through neglect. It is not just a messy room or ordinary dirt. Squalor is when a place (or sometimes a situation) has deteriorated to a level that feels deeply wretched, unhealthy, and unfit for human beings.

Think of it this way: if a room hasn't been cleaned in weeks, that's messy. If a room hasn't been cleaned in years, is crawling with insects, smells of rotting food, has mold creeping up the walls, and broken things lying everywhere — that is squalor.

The word carries three connected ideas at once, and understanding all three gives you full command of it.

1. Extreme physical filth
This is the most visible layer. Squalor describes conditions that are not just unclean but shockingly, offensively dirty. We're talking about accumulated grime, waste, decay, and neglect — the kind of filth that makes people recoil.

2. Prolonged neglect
Squalor doesn't happen overnight. It implies that things have been left to rot, crumble, or decay over a long period with no one caring for them. A place falls into squalor. It is the result of long abandonment or indifference.

3. Human degradation and wretchedness
This is what truly sets "squalor" apart from a word like "filth." Squalor almost always carries a sense of misery and loss of dignity, especially when people are living in it. It suggests conditions that are beneath what any human being should have to endure. This is why the word appears so often in the context of extreme poverty, neglect, or suffering. It's not just a description of a dirty place — it's a judgment that something has gone terribly, sadly wrong.

To sharpen your understanding, here's what the word does not mean:

  • A messy desk is not squalor. Squalor is extreme and pervasive, not just untidy.
  • Ordinary poverty is not squalor. A person can be very poor and still live in a clean, dignified home. Squalor is specifically about the physical condition of filth and neglect.
  • A dirty car or unwashed dishes is not squalor. The scale and severity of squalor is much greater — it overwhelms a space entirely.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Squalor" is a powerful word. It is not neutral. When you use it, you are communicating not just a fact (this place is dirty) but an emotional response to that fact — shock, sadness, disgust, or moral concern. Writers and journalists use it deliberately to make readers feel the weight of what they are describing.

It is the kind of word that signals: this is serious. This is not acceptable. This is suffering.

These examples will show you how the word behaves in real use:

  • "Rescue workers found the elderly man living in complete squalor — the house had no electricity, no clean water, and the floors were buried under years of rubbish."
  • "She had escaped the squalor of her childhood neighborhood and built a new life for herself."
  • "The report described the conditions in the overcrowded prison as squalor unfit for animals, let alone human beings."
  • "After the factory closed, the surrounding town slowly sank into economic despair and urban squalor."
  • "The charity's mission is to rescue children from poverty and squalor."

• "Live in squalor" — the most common use; means to exist in these wretched, filthy conditions.
  • "Abject squalor" — abject means total and complete; this phrase intensifies the word to mean the most extreme, hopeless kind of squalor imaginable.
  • "Filth and squalor" — these two words are often paired together for emphasis.
  • "Fall into squalor" — means a place has gradually deteriorated to this state.
  • "Urban squalor" — refers to these conditions specifically in a city environment, often in the context of neglected neighborhoods or slums.
If you ever need to recall this word quickly: squalor is the state of living in extreme, wretched filth and neglect — a condition so degrading that it implies human suffering, not just a dirty space.
15068:
To squander something means to waste it in a careless, reckless, or foolish way — particularly something that was valuable and could have been used much better.

Three things are always true when this word applies: the thing being wasted had real value, there was a smarter or better way to use it, and the person used it up carelessly with little or nothing good to show for it afterward.
What makes squander different from simply "wasting" something

The word carries a strong sense of avoidable loss. When you say someone squandered something, you are implying that they had a genuine choice — they could have used it well — but instead they threw it away through foolishness, laziness, recklessness, or poor decisions. The loss is on them.

This is also why squander is not the same as losing something. If your wallet gets stolen, you lost your money — it was taken from you. But if you blow your entire salary on lottery tickets, you squandered it — you caused the waste through your own choices. The word always points the finger at the person who had the thing and failed to use it wisely.
What kinds of things get squandered?

The word is most naturally used with things that are valuable and finite — things you only get a limited amount of.

Money is the most classic example. Someone who inherits a fortune and spends it all on frivolous, useless things within a few years has squandered their inheritance.

Time is another. If a student has an entire summer to study for an important exam but spends every day doing nothing, they have squandered those months.

Opportunities are frequently squandered. If you are offered a rare chance — a great job, a meeting with someone powerful, a scholarship — and you fail to take it seriously or let it slip away through carelessness, you have squandered that opportunity.

Talent can be squandered too. Someone born with an extraordinary natural gift — for music, sport, mathematics — but who never develops or uses it through laziness or distraction has squandered their talent.

In sports, a team that builds up a large lead and then plays so poorly that they lose the game is said to have squandered their lead.

Squander is not mild or neutral. It carries real emotional weight — a sense of disappointment, regret, and moral judgment. It suggests not just that something was wasted, but that it was wasted badly, in a way that was foolish and should have been avoided. This is why the word often appears when people are looking back sadly at missed chances or shaking their heads at poor decisions.
How it compares to similar words

Waste is the closest synonym and can often be used in its place. But squander is stronger and more dramatic. It implies a greater degree of foolishness and a more significant thing being lost.

Spend is a neutral word — you can spend money wisely or unwisely. Squander is always negative. You can never squander something wisely.

Fritter away means something similar to squander, but it usually suggests small, gradual losses over time — like frittering away hours on your phone, bit by bit. Squander can apply to both gradual waste and one big, dramatic loss.

Misuse means putting something to the wrong purpose. Squander means burning through something with little or nothing meaningful to show for it at the end.
Sentences to see it in action

"He squandered his entire inheritance within two years and was left with nothing."

"She squandered her youth watching television instead of building toward her dreams."

"Don't squander this opportunity — a chance like this rarely comes twice."

"The team squandered a commanding lead and ended up losing in the final minutes."

"He had a brilliant mind but squandered his talent by never applying himself to anything."

"Years of good health were squandered on bad habits."
The person who squanders things is called a squanderer. The ongoing act of wasting is called squandering. You might say: "His squandering of company funds led to the firm's collapse."
A simple mental check for when to use it

Ask yourself: Was the thing valuable? Was there a better way to use it? Did the person waste it carelessly through their own choices, with nothing worthwhile to show for it? If the answer to all three is yes, squander is exactly the right word.
15069:
"Square away" means to organize, settle, or take care of something so that it is completely in order and ready. Think of it as tying up all the loose ends — making sure nothing is left messy, unfinished, or unsettled.

It can apply to physical things (like a room), abstract things (like plans or finances), situations (like a problem), or even people (making sure someone has everything they need).

This idiom has its roots in sailing and the navy, which is why it sounds a little old-fashioned and serious.

On old sailing ships, the sails were attached to long horizontal poles called yards. When sailors adjusted these yards so that they stood at a perfect right angle (90°) to the ship — both with the mast and with the direction of the wind — the ship was in its ideal, ready-to-sail position. This position was called "square" because everything was geometrically lined up and correct.

When the captain gave the order to "square away," it meant: set the sails properly, get everything in order, and make the ship ready. The ship was no longer drifting or adjusting — it was set, organized, and good to go.

Over time, this nautical idea jumped from ships into everyday English, and people started using it to describe any situation where things are properly organized, settled, and under control.
The Two Main Forms and Their Meanings

This idiom is used in two main ways, and it helps to understand both separately.

Form 1: "Square away" (as a verb)

When used as a verb, it means to organize, settle, or handle something — the act of doing it.

Pattern: square away + something

Examples:

  • "I need to square away my finances before the end of the month."
    I need to get my finances sorted out and in order.
  • "Let's square away the details of the project before we begin."
    Let's settle and finalize all the details first.
  • "She spent the morning squaring away her desk before the big presentation."
    She spent the morning tidying and organizing her desk.
  • "Can you square away the travel bookings for next week?"
    Can you handle and finalize the travel arrangements?

Form 2: "Squared away" (as an adjective)

When used as an adjective, "squared away" describes a state — the state of being organized, settled, and taken care of. It means everything is already done and in order.

Pattern: is/are/be + squared away

Examples:

  • "Don't worry — everything is squared away."
    Everything is handled and in perfect order. There's nothing left to worry about.
  • "Are the new employees squared away with their paperwork?"
    Have the new employees finished and sorted out all their paperwork?
  • "I'll leave once I'm sure you're squared away."
    I'll leave once I'm sure you have everything you need and everything is fine.

A special use of "squared away" in the military

In military culture — especially in the U.S. military — "squared away" is also used to describe a person who is disciplined, reliable, sharp, and has everything under control. It's a compliment meaning the person is highly organized and together.

  • "He's a squared away soldier."
    He is disciplined, organized, and has his act completely together.

This usage carries a strong sense of respect and professionalism.
The Key Feeling Behind the Idiom

The heart of "square away" is the idea of completeness and readiness. Just like the old ship with its sails perfectly set — nothing is crooked, nothing is missing, nothing is left undone. Everything is where it should be.

So whenever you hear "square away," think: Is everything organized, settled, and taken care of? Yes? Then it's squared away.
How It Compares to Similar Phrases

To help you lock in the meaning, here are phrases that carry a very similar meaning to "square away":

  • Sort out → "I need to sort out the finances." (very close in meaning)
  • Take care of → "Let me take care of the details."
  • Wrap up → "We need to wrap up the loose ends."
  • Get in order → "Get everything in order before we leave."
  • Tie up loose ends → similar idea of finishing off remaining things

The difference is that "square away" often emphasizes complete orderliness — not just doing something, but making sure it is properly, cleanly done with nothing left hanging.

Core meaningTo organize, settle, or handle something so it is completely in order
As a verbThe act of sorting/settling something — "square away the details"
As an adjectiveThe state of being organized and handled — "everything is squared away"
OriginNautical — setting a ship's sails at the correct right angle so it is ready to sail
ToneSlightly formal, often used in American English, common in military settings
Similar to"Sort out," "take care of," "get in order"

The next time someone says "once we're squared away, we can move forward," you'll know exactly what they mean: once everything is properly organized, settled, and ready — with nothing left loose or unfinished — then they can proceed.
